title: When the Checkout Request Becomes a Battle | Parenting Rewind
audience_intent: Adults and parents; not directed to children
education_scope: General parenting education only; not personalised therapy, diagnosis, or medical advice.

narration.transcript: The checkout display appears, your five-year-old asks for a treat, and the line behind you keeps moving. A long explanation can become an accidental negotiation when the answer has already been decided. Pause, get close, and choose two options you can genuinely accept. Say: We are not buying checkout sweets today; you may help place the apples on the belt or hold the shopping list. A short direction and two bounded choices give the child a useful next action without changing the limit.

source.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source.title: Tips for Giving Directions

claim_limits: Suggested wording is an example, not a guaranteed result.
